title: Social Prescribing to Improve Access to Health and Care Services for People in Vulnerable Situations: An International, Multicentre, Pragmatic, Individually Randomised Controlled Basket Trial
summary:
Background

Many people live in difficult life situations that can affect their health and well-being. These include, for example, loneliness, financial difficulties, housing problems, family-related challenges, or a lack of social support. Such social problems can have a strong influence on how healthy people feel and how well they manage everyday life.

In many cities and communities, helpful support services are available, such as counselling services, group activities, social initiatives, or volunteering opportunities. Although these services exist, they are often not well connected to medical care. People in vulnerable situations in particular may not know about these services or may find it difficult to access them.

For many individuals, the general practitioner is the first point of contact when facing problems. However, in everyday practice there is often limited time or opportunity to help patients find suitable non-medical support.

Research question

This study investigates whether Social Prescribing can help people in vulnerable life situations to better find and use suitable community-based support services. In addition, the study examines whether Social Prescribing can improve participants’ well-being, quality of life, and social situation.

Methods

Adults are invited to take part in the study through their general practitioner. The study focuses on individuals with social problems affecting their health who belong to particularly vulnerable groups, including LGBTQ+ persons, refugees and first-generation migrants, and older adults living alone.

All participants take part in telephone interviews at the beginning of the study and again after six and twelve months. The intervention group receives support through Social Prescribing. Participants in this group are referred to link workers, who take time to talk with them about their situation, help them set personal goals, and support them in finding and accessing suitable community-based services, such as counselling, group activities, or social initiatives.

The control group continues to receive usual care from their general practitioner.

The study then compares how often community-based support services are used and how participants’ well-being and life situation change over time.
conditions: Non-Medical health related social needs (International Classification of Primary Care 3rd Edition, ICPC-3: ZC01-ZC99 “Social Problems”)

interventions.name: Social Prescribing (SP) is a structured, non-medical intervention. Eligible participants are referred by their general practitioner (GP) to a trained link worker. The link worker assesses the participant’s health-related social needs, jointly defines individual goals, and develops a personalised act
Usual care, supplemented by an information brochure on locally available, non-clinical, community-based support services (Care-As-Usual+, CAU+).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- Presence of at least one non-medical, health-related social need according to Chapter ZC of the International Classification of Primary Care, 3rd Revision (ICPC-3)
- Belonging to at least one of the following target groups: (1) LGBTQ+ persons, (2) refugees or first-generation migrants, or (3) older adults living alone (aged 65 years or older)
- Ability to provide informed consent
- Basic language skills sufficient to participate in the study
Exclusion criteria:
- Participation in another psychosocial intervention study
- Legal guardianship for health-related decisions
- Another person from the same household already participating in the study
- Study staff or employees of participating study centres and their immediate family members
